title: SCSS Linting
learning_outcomes: Explain scss linting and connect it to at least two of its syllabus subtopics.
Apply scss linting in a small SCSS example and predict the resulting CSS or compiler behavior.
Inspect the output, diagnose one plausible mistake, and state a relevant limitation or best practice.

content.intro: This lesson turns **SCSS Linting** into a practical, inspectable step. You will connect why linting matters with enforcing style conventions, then check what Dart Sass emits instead of relying on the SCSS source alone.
content.why_it_matters: A stylesheet is correct only when it compiles and behaves correctly in the target browser and interface. Keep the source, compiler diagnostics, generated CSS, and rendered page available while debugging.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Start with the smallest source file that demonstrates scss linting. 2. State what should change and what should stay the same. 3. Compile the entrypoint with Dart Sass, or use the stated command if this lesson is about the toolchain. 4. Compare the resulting CSS or diagnostic with the expected result, then change one input and repeat.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: SCSS Linting
content_blocks.expected_output: A lint configuration makes chosen style conventions repeatable; confirm the exact rule is supported by the installed linter version.
content_blocks.execution_note: This course example is a Sass/SCSS or tooling example. CodeLeaf’s current in-browser playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only; compile Sass locally with Dart Sass. Do not treat the browser preview as a Sass compiler.

content_blocks.title: Modern Sass note
content_blocks.text: Use Dart Sass for new work. Prefer @use / @forward and namespaced sass: built-in modules. Sass compiles to CSS; browser-native CSS features still run in the browser.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Audit a small stylesheet for scss linting. Save the original source and compiled CSS, make one deliberate change, recompile, and write down the evidence that the change is correct and safe.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Do not edit generated CSS when you intend to change source behavior. Edit the SCSS entrypoint or its module, compile again, and compare the generated output.

task: Audit a small stylesheet for scss linting. Save the original source and compiled CSS, make one deliberate change, recompile, and write down the evidence that the change is correct and safe.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example includes the intended Sass construct and a clear input.
The expected output or tool result is documented and consistent with the source.
The work is reproducible and includes one limitation, test, or troubleshooting note.
hints: Reduce the example to one source file and one entrypoint before adding more abstractions.
Read the first compiler diagnostic and confirm you are editing the Sass source, not only generated CSS.
Compile and inspect the emitted CSS; compare exact selectors, values, and at-rules with your expectation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming SCSS runs directly in the browser.
common_mistakes.why: Browsers consume CSS, not Sass syntax.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with Dart Sass and load the resulting .css file in the HTML page.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting source readability without inspecting generated output.
common_mistakes.why: Nesting, mixins, loops, and extension can emit unexpected selectors or more CSS than intended.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile a small example and inspect the CSS output or browser computed styles.
